notes.meaning: People from the town of Ziph come to Saul's hometown of Gibeah to betray David a second time. They report that David is hiding on the hill of Hachilah, likely hoping to win the king's favor and protect themselves from David's men. Even though Saul had previously wept and admitted David was righteous, this tip reignites the king's jealousy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that chapters 24 and 26 are two different tellings of the very same historical event preserved by separate oral traditions.

notes.meaning: Saul immediately breaks his earlier promises and sets out with three thousand picked troops. This large force was his regular standing army of skilled soldiers, vastly outnumbering David's small band of six hundred men. Saul's quick relapse shows how easily an unrepentant heart loses its good intentions.

Saul camps by the road near the hill, while David remains hidden deeper in the wilderness. When David hears of Saul's movements, he sends out scouts to confirm the king's exact position before making a move. David acts prudently to defend his men rather than rushing into an ambush.

David goes in person to inspect Saul's camp and sees where the king and his general, Abner, are resting. Saul sleeps in the center of the camp, safely ringed by his supply wagons and his soldiers. Seeing this layout with his own eyes prepares David for his daring night visit.

David asks two companions who will dare to sneak down into the royal camp with him under cover of darkness. Ahimelech the Hittite, a foreign recruit who had joined David, remains silent, but Abishai steps up at once. Abishai is David's nephew, the son of his sister Zeruiah, and already known for his bold courage.

David and Abishai slip right into the camp at night while all the soldiers are asleep. They find Saul lying in the middle of the camp with his royal spear stuck in the ground right by his head, and his general Abner sleeping nearby. Saul is totally helpless, leaving his life completely exposed to his pursuers.

Abishai whispers that God has handed Saul over to David and begs for permission to kill him on the spot. He promises to pin Saul to the earth with a single thrust of the spear so the king cannot even cry out. To Abishai, this open opportunity looks like God's clear sign to end their running and take the throne.

David firmly stops Abishai from harming Saul. He insists that no one can strike the Lord's anointed—the king chosen and set apart with holy oil by God's command—and remain innocent of sin. Even though Saul is acting like an enemy, David refuses to take the throne through murder or rebellion.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers use the phrase 'touch not the Lord's anointed' to claim that church leaders should never be questioned or corrected by church members.

notes.meaning: David swears an oath that God Himself will deal with Saul in His own time and way. He lists the only proper ways Saul's life will end: struck down by God's judgment, dying of natural old age, or falling in battle against Israel's enemies. David leaves vengeance entirely to God instead of taking matters into his own hands.

David repeats his refusal to lay a hand on God's anointed king, choosing instead to take Saul's spear and water jug. The spear was the symbol of Saul's royal authority, and the jug held the water needed to survive in the dry desert. Taking them provides clear physical proof of where David stood without causing any harm to Saul.

David takes the royal spear and water jug from beside Saul's head, and the two men slip quietly away into the night. Not a single guard wakes up, stirs, or spots them because God had placed an unusually heavy sleep over the entire camp. God protected David and provided this peaceful demonstration of David's innocence.

David climbs to the top of a mountain on the opposite side of the valley, putting a wide gorge between himself and Saul's camp. The steep ravine keeps him safe from any sudden attack, while the still night air allows his voice to carry across the open space. From this secure distance, he prepares to call out to the army.

David shouts across the valley to the army and calls out Abner by name until the commander finally wakes up. Abner groggily answers and demands to know who is making such a loud disturbance near the king. He does not yet realize who is calling or that the camp has been breached.

David mocks Abner with sharp irony, asking why such a famous and mighty commander failed to guard his master. He points out that an intruder had entered the camp with the power to destroy the king, yet the guards were fast asleep. David shows that he cared more for Saul's safety than the king's own general did.

David tells Abner that failing to guard the Lord's anointed king is a terrible failure of duty worthy of death under military law. To prove what happened, David tells the soldiers to look around and notice that Saul's royal spear and water jug are missing from beside his head. The missing items stand as undeniable evidence that Saul's life was spared.

Saul wakes up, recognizes David's familiar voice in the morning light, and asks if it is really his 'son' David calling out. David replies with great respect, addressing Saul as his master and rightful king. Even while defending himself, David maintains proper honor toward the ruler who is hunting him.

David asks Saul plainly why he continues to chase a loyal servant who has committed no crime. He challenges the king to name any evil deed or treason David has actually done. David speaks with the clear conscience of a man whose hands are completely clean.

David urges Saul to consider the real reason behind this pursuit: if God stirred Saul up to discipline David, David is ready to offer a sacrifice for peace; but if wicked advisers spread lies, they deserve God's curse. By driving David out of the promised land, his enemies were effectively cutting him off from the worship of God and pushing him toward foreign idols. David grieves the loss of fellowship with God's people far more than the loss of earthly comfort.

David pleads that his life not be wasted on foreign soil, far away from the sanctuary of the Lord. He compares himself to something harmless like a single flea, or a wild partridge that hunters endlessly chase over the mountains until it collapses from exhaustion. He points out how unworthy it is for the king of Israel to bring an army of thousands just to hunt down an innocent man.

Saul openly confesses that he has sinned, invites David to return home, and promises never to hurt him again because David spared his life. He admits that he has acted like a fool and made a terrible, tragic mistake. While Saul feels genuine regret in this emotional moment, his past behavior gives David no real reason to trust his word.

David holds up the royal spear and tells Saul to send one of his young soldiers across the ravine to collect it. David wisely refuses to bring it back himself, knowing he cannot safely place himself in Saul's power again. Returning the spear shows that David has no desire to steal the throne by force.

David prays that the Lord will reward every person according to their righteousness and faithfulness. He notes that God handed Saul over to him that day, yet he refused to raise his hand against the Lord's anointed king. David relies on God's justice rather than Saul's unstable promises.

David expresses his hope that just as he treated Saul's life as precious and spared it, so the Lord will value David's life and rescue him from all trouble. David places his ultimate security in God's hands rather than expecting fair treatment from the king. His trust rests entirely on God's mercy and protection.

Saul pronounces a blessing over David, acknowledging that David will achieve great things and ultimately triumph. With those words, the two men part ways and never meet again in Scripture; David goes his way in the wilderness, and Saul travels back home to Gibeah. David's patient trust in God preserved his integrity until God opened the way to the kingdom.
